about: Gap-fill inventory (2026-11-08): treatments the finder found for interview topics the first seven inventories lack (dossiers/gap-patterns.md), and open prose for concepts that had none (sweep-dsa.md, sweep-system-design.md). Each row's id and locator carry its real source prefix; the source is the registry row whose locator scheme has that prefix. Every locator was checked against sources/_cache/<id>/.

concepts.name: Two pointers
concepts.statement: Two indices move through an array, typically from both ends of a sorted array toward each other, so that each step discards one candidate and a pair with a target sum (or the best pair) is found in one O(n) pass with O(1) extra space.
concepts.notes: E (short): docstring essay on what the technique is, its O(n)/O(1) cost and when to use it, then commented pair-sum code on a sorted array. The LeetCode links at the end are link-only.

concepts.name: Pair sum in a sorted array by two pointers
concepts.statement: In a sorted array, start i at the left and j at the right; if a[i]+a[j] is too small move i right, if too large move j left. No discarded pair can be the answer, so the scan finds it in O(n).
concepts.notes: A: why moving one end is safe, with complexity. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Container with most water by two pointers
concepts.statement: With pointers at both ends, the area is limited by the shorter line; moving the shorter side inward is the only move that can improve the area, so one inward scan finds the maximum in O(n).
concepts.notes: A: move the shorter side inward; reasoning and complexity. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Two pointers on a sorted sequence
concepts.statement: Sortedness makes two pointers correct: for a target pair sum, if num[l]+num[r] > target decrease r, if smaller increase l; the pointers close in on the answer in O(n), beating binary search by a log factor.
concepts.notes: E: the page's introduction (引入) defines two pointers as moving together or toward each other; this section works the sorted pair-sum case. Chinese; usable in translation under docs/prompts/translate.md, AI-marked as a translation; SATA attribution thanks the OI Wiki authors (ruling 15).

concepts.name: 3SUM in quadratic time
concepts.statement: Sort the array; for each a[i], look for a pair summing to -a[i] in the rest with two pointers moving inward by the sign of the sum, giving O(n^2) time.
concepts.notes: E: colour-coded trace on a small array and a correctness argument. The sort is used as a black box (sorting is chapter 10).

concepts.name: 3SUM by sorting and two pointers, skipping duplicates
concepts.statement: Sort, fix i, run two pointers on the suffix, and skip equal neighbours so that each triple is reported once; O(n^2) time.
concepts.notes: A. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Merging two sorted lists
concepts.statement: Two sorted lists are merged by keeping one pointer in each and repeatedly moving the smaller head to the output, in time linear in the total length.
concepts.notes: E: pseudocode and linear cost; the merge that merge sort repeats.

concepts.name: Floyd's tortoise and hare
concepts.statement: Move one pointer one step and another two steps along x_i = f(x_{i-1}); they meet inside the cycle, and restarting one pointer from the start finds the cycle's first element.
concepts.notes: E. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Finding a cycle in a singly linked list with two pointers
concepts.statement: A slow pointer moving one node and a fast pointer moving two meet iff the list has a cycle; resetting one to the head and moving both one step finds the cycle entry.
concepts.notes: E. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows. Chinese; usable in translation under docs/prompts/translate.md, AI-marked as a translation; SATA attribution thanks the OI Wiki authors (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Duplicate number by Floyd cycle detection
concepts.statement: Reading an array of n+1 values in 1..n as a function i -> a[i] makes the duplicate the entry of a cycle, which tortoise and hare find in O(n) time and O(1) space.
concepts.locator: algo-explanation:Search Algorithms/Floyd Cycle Detection Algorithm to Find Duplicate Number
concepts.notes: E (MIT prose, ruling 12): fast/slow pointers on an array-as-function. Embedded images are hot-linked and link-only. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Dutch national flag (three-way) partition
concepts.statement: Dijkstra's three-way partition keeps three indices i, j, k so that the array holds values below, equal to and above the pivot, in one pass and in place.
concepts.notes: E: pseudocode. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Fixed-size sliding window
concepts.statement: A window of the last k items is updated in O(1) per step by adding the item that enters and subtracting the one that leaves (SMA_next = SMA_prev + (p_new - p_old)/k), instead of recomputing all k.
concepts.notes: E: derives the O(1) update; the buffer of the last k items is a FIFO queue.

concepts.name: Sliding window
concepts.statement: A sliding window is a contiguous range of fixed size moved one position at a time over an array or string; it turns nested loops over subarrays into one pass.
concepts.notes: E (short, fixed windows only): definition, cost, when to use; the code lists windows by slicing and names longest-substring and maximum-sum-of-size-k as uses.

concepts.name: Maximum average subarray of length k
concepts.statement: Keep the sum of the current length-k window, add the entering element and subtract the leaving one, and track the maximum sum: O(n) time, O(1) space.
concepts.notes: A. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Most vowels in a substring of length k
concepts.statement: Count the vowels in the first k characters, then slide the window one step at a time, adjusting the count for the entering and leaving characters.
concepts.notes: A. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Permutation in a string by a window of counts
concepts.statement: A window of length |s1| over s2 keeps character counts; it contains a permutation of s1 exactly when its counts equal those of s1, and each slide changes two counts.
concepts.notes: A: fixed window of counts. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: All anagram windows of a pattern
concepts.statement: Slide a length-|p| window over s with an array of character counts and report every start where the counts match those of p.
concepts.notes: A: fixed window of counts. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Variable-size sliding window
concepts.statement: Extend the window at the right one element at a time and shrink it from the left while it breaks the condition (here: a repeated character, tracked in a set), so each element enters and leaves once and the longest valid window is found in O(n).
concepts.notes: A: longest substring without repeats. The write-up keeps the window's characters in a hash set (hash tables are chapter 5). Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Minimum window substring
concepts.statement: Grow the window until it covers every needed character count, then shrink it from the left while it still covers them, recording the shortest window; O(m+n).
concepts.notes: A: the minimum covering window, a shrink-while-valid window. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Shortest subarray with sum at least the target
concepts.statement: With positive numbers, extend the right end, and while the window sum is at least the target record its length and move the left end; O(n).
concepts.notes: A. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Maintaining window information with two pointers
concepts.statement: Two pointers l and r maintain information about [l, r] that is monotone and cheap to update when one element enters or leaves (a sum of positives, a product of positive integers): advance r, then advance l until the window is valid again; for each r the count of valid windows ending there is r-l+1.
concepts.notes: E: the general expand/shrink account with two worked examples (LeetCode 713 statement quoted; the explanation is OI Wiki's). Chinese; usable in translation under docs/prompts/translate.md, AI-marked as a translation; SATA attribution thanks the OI Wiki authors (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Longest substring with at most k distinct characters
concepts.statement: A map from character to last index maintains a window; when it holds more than k characters, drop the one with the lowest index and move the left end past it.
concepts.notes: A: the solution notebook's "## Algorithm" section (Apache-2.0 prose, ruling 12). The online_judges copy is link-only.

concepts.name: Monotonic queue for sliding-window minimum
concepts.statement: A deque holding the window's candidates in increasing order gives the minimum of every length-k window in O(n) total, against O(nk) naively and O(n log n) with a heap; the same structure is a min-queue.
concepts.notes: E: pseudocode and comparison with the naive and heap methods. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Sliding window maximum with a monotonic deque
concepts.statement: Keep indices in a deque with decreasing values, pop from the back before pushing, pop the front when it leaves the window; the front is the window maximum, O(n) total.
concepts.notes: A: Solution 1 of the same write-up uses a heap. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Monotonic queue
concepts.statement: A monotonic queue keeps the elements that can still be the window minimum (or maximum) in order; sliding the window pops expired elements from the front and dominated ones from the back, giving every window's extreme in O(n).
concepts.notes: E: introduced on the sliding-window problem, then defined and analysed. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows. Chinese; usable in translation under docs/prompts/translate.md, AI-marked as a translation; SATA attribution thanks the OI Wiki authors (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Prefix sums
concepts.statement: The prefix sums of x_0, x_1, ... are y_i = x_0 + ... + x_i, computed in one pass by y_i = y_{i-1} + x_i; with them any range sum is a difference of two prefix sums, and finite differences invert them.
concepts.notes: E (definition): the lead and the inclusive/exclusive scan section; the range-sum use is stated briefly.

concepts.name: Prefix sum array for range queries
concepts.statement: Precompute prefix[i] = a[0]+...+a[i] once in O(n); then the sum of a[l..r] is prefix[r] - prefix[l-1], answered in O(1).
concepts.notes: E (short): docstring essay and code.

concepts.name: Range sum query with a leading zero
concepts.statement: Store s with s[0] = 0 and s[i+1] = s[i] + nums[i]; the sum of nums[l..r] is s[r+1] - s[l], with no special case at l = 0.
concepts.notes: A/E. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: One-dimensional prefix sums
concepts.statement: S_i = a_1 + ... + a_i is built by the recurrence S_i = S_{i-1} + a_i in O(n), after which the sum of a_l..a_r is S_r - S_{l-1}.
concepts.notes: E: worked example with code. Chinese; usable in translation under docs/prompts/translate.md, AI-marked as a translation; SATA attribution thanks the OI Wiki authors (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Two-dimensional prefix sums (summed-area table)
concepts.statement: I(x, y) = i(x, y) + I(x, y-1) + I(x-1, y) - I(x-1, y-1) builds the table in one pass, after which the sum over any axis-aligned rectangle takes four lookups by inclusion-exclusion.
concepts.notes: E: one-pass build and four-corner query. The figure File:Summed area table.png has an unchecked licence.

concepts.name: Range sum query 2D by prefix sums
concepts.statement: s[i+1][j+1] = s[i][j+1] + s[i+1][j] - s[i][j] + matrix[i][j]; a submatrix sum is s[x2+1][y2+1] - s[x1][y2+1] - s[x2+1][y1] + s[x1][y1].
concepts.notes: A/E. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Two-dimensional prefix sums by inclusion-exclusion
concepts.statement: S_{i,j} = a_{i,j} + S_{i-1,j} + S_{i,j-1} - S_{i-1,j-1}, and a sub-rectangle sum is recovered by the same inclusion-exclusion with four terms.
concepts.notes: E: with a figure (prefix-sum-2d.svg, part of the BY-SA page) and an example. Chinese; usable in translation under docs/prompts/translate.md, AI-marked as a translation; SATA attribution thanks the OI Wiki authors (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Difference arrays
concepts.statement: The difference array b_i = a_i - a_{i-1} is the inverse of prefix sums: adding v to a_l..a_r becomes b_l += v and b_{r+1} -= v, so many range updates cost O(1) each and one prefix-sum pass recovers the array.
concepts.notes: E: the only general account of difference arrays found; with an example. Chinese; usable in translation under docs/prompts/translate.md, AI-marked as a translation; SATA attribution thanks the OI Wiki authors (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Range addition by a difference array
concepts.statement: For each update (l, r, v) do d[l] += v and d[r+1] -= v; the prefix sums of d are the final array, O(n + k) for k updates.
concepts.notes: A/E: Solution 2 of the same write-up adds a Fenwick tree. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Car pooling by a difference array over positions
concepts.statement: Add each trip's passengers at its start and subtract them at its end in a difference array over positions; the prefix sums give the load at every point, which must never exceed capacity.
concepts.notes: A. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Flight bookings by a difference array
concepts.statement: Each booking (first, last, seats) adds seats to a range of flights; record it as two difference-array updates and take prefix sums once.
concepts.notes: A. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Two-dimensional difference arrays
concepts.statement: Adding v to every cell of a sub-rectangle becomes four point updates of a 2D difference array (+v, -v, -v, +v at the corners), and a 2D prefix-sum pass recovers the matrix.
concepts.notes: E. Chinese; usable in translation under docs/prompts/translate.md, AI-marked as a translation; SATA attribution thanks the OI Wiki authors (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Kahn's algorithm
concepts.statement: Put every vertex with no incoming edge in a set S; repeatedly remove a vertex from S, append it to the order, delete its out-edges and add any vertex left with no incoming edge. If edges remain at the end the graph has a cycle; otherwise the order is topological, found in O(V+E).
concepts.notes: E: pseudocode, cycle detection by leftover edges, O(V+E); S may be a set, queue or stack.

concepts.name: Queue-based topological sort
concepts.statement: Count each vertex's incoming edges, queue the vertices whose count is zero, and when a vertex leaves the queue print it and decrement its neighbours' counts, queueing those that reach zero; if the queue empties before every vertex is printed, the graph has a cycle.
concepts.notes: E (MIT prose, ruling 12): with the topSortQCON slideshow (MIT JavaScript, not cached). The same module's depth-first solution duplicates topological-sort.

concepts.name: Course schedule by Kahn's algorithm
concepts.statement: Build the prerequisite graph with an in-degree array, process zero in-degree courses from a queue, and decide that all courses can be finished iff every course is processed.
concepts.notes: A. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Course schedule order by Kahn's algorithm
concepts.statement: The order in which Kahn's algorithm removes zero in-degree vertices is a valid course order; return it, or an empty list if some course is never removed.
concepts.notes: A (short). Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Kahn's algorithm
concepts.statement: Maintain the set S of vertices with in-degree 0; take one out, append it to the order, and delete its out-edges, adding vertices whose in-degree becomes 0; O(V+E), and a vertex never reaching in-degree 0 shows a cycle. Using a priority queue for S gives the lexicographically smallest order.
concepts.notes: E: process, complexity, implementation; the same page has the DFS method and lexicographically smallest/largest orders. Chinese; usable in translation under docs/prompts/translate.md, AI-marked as a translation; SATA attribution thanks the OI Wiki authors (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Build order by repeatedly removing independent nodes
concepts.statement: Process the projects with no remaining dependencies, remove their outgoing edges, and repeat; if at some step no project is free, there is a circular dependency. O(V+E).
concepts.notes: A: the solution notebook's "## Algorithm" section (Apache-2.0 prose, ruling 12).

concepts.name: Topological sort by repeatedly taking a minimal element
concepts.statement: In a finite DAG, repeatedly picking a minimal vertex (one not reachable from any other remaining vertex) and removing it lists the vertices in a topological order; so every finite DAG has a topological sort.
concepts.notes: E (mathematical, no data structures): the getting-dressed DAG. It is Kahn's idea stated as an existence proof, so it treats the existence of topological orders, not the O(V+E) algorithm. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Topological sort as repeated selection of a minimal element
concepts.statement: Every nonempty finite partial order has a minimal element (by induction), so putting a minimal element first and sorting the rest extends any finite partial order to a total order.
concepts.notes: E (mathematical; efficiency explicitly skipped). Treats the existence of topological orders. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Unweighted interval scheduling: earliest finish first
concepts.statement: Repeatedly selecting the interval with the earliest finishing time and discarding those that overlap it yields a maximum set of pairwise compatible intervals; other natural greedy rules fail.
concepts.notes: E. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Activity selection: greedy by finish time
concepts.statement: Sort activities by finish time and take each one that starts after the last selected one finishes; an exchange argument (Proof of optimality) shows the greedy set is maximum. O(n log n).
concepts.notes: E: pseudocode, explanation and proof of optimality in the following subsections. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Activity selection problem
concepts.statement: Sort activities by finishing time and repeatedly select the next activity compatible with those chosen; worked on a class timetable.
concepts.notes: E: carry the chapter's contributor credits; images link-only. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Interval scheduling: which greedy works
concepts.statement: Of four candidate greedy orders (earliest start, shortest, fewest conflicts, earliest finish), counterexamples rule out the first three; earliest finish time is optimal.
concepts.notes: E: images link-only; carry the contributor credits. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Fewest intervals to remove for no overlap
concepts.statement: Sort by end and keep each interval that starts at or after the last kept end; the number removed is n minus the maximum set of non-overlapping intervals.
concepts.notes: A. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Merging overlapping intervals
concepts.statement: Sort intervals by start; scan them, extending the current merged interval while the next one starts no later than its end, and starting a new one otherwise. O(n log n).
concepts.notes: A/E: Solutions 2 and 3 of the same write-up are variants. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Inserting an interval into sorted disjoint intervals
concepts.statement: Copy the intervals that end before the new one, merge every interval that overlaps it into one, then copy the rest; one pass, O(n).
concepts.notes: A. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Checking whether intervals overlap
concepts.statement: After sorting by start, a set of intervals is pairwise disjoint iff every interval starts no earlier than its predecessor ends.
concepts.notes: A (short): the overlap test that merging rests on. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Minimum meeting rooms as maximum overlap
concepts.statement: Add +1 at each meeting's start and -1 at its end in a difference array over time; the largest prefix sum is the largest number of meetings in progress at once, which is the minimum number of rooms.
concepts.notes: A: Solution 2 of the same write-up does the same sweep with a sorted map of events. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Generating all permutations by backtracking
concepts.statement: Fill positions one at a time; at each position try every unused element (tracked in a used-array), recurse, then undo the choice. n! permutations, each produced in O(n).
concepts.notes: A/E. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Permutations of a multiset by backtracking
concepts.statement: Sort the input; when choosing the element for a position, skip an element equal to the previous one unless that one is in use, so each distinct permutation is generated once.
concepts.notes: A. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Permutations of a string with duplicates
concepts.statement: Keep a count per distinct character; at each step choose any character with a positive count, decrement it, recurse, and restore it, which yields each distinct permutation once. O(n!) results.
concepts.notes: A: the solution notebook's "## Algorithm" section (Apache-2.0 prose, ruling 12).

concepts.name: Next permutation in lexicographic order
concepts.statement: Find the largest k with a[k] < a[k+1], then the largest l > k with a[k] < a[l]; swap them and reverse a[k+1..]. Repeating from the sorted order lists all permutations lexicographically, and repeated values are handled.
concepts.notes: E: step list.

concepts.name: Next permutation by two traversals
concepts.statement: Scan from the right for the first i with nums[i] < nums[i+1], scan again for the rightmost j with nums[j] > nums[i], swap, and reverse the suffix after i; O(n), in place.
concepts.notes: A. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Heap's algorithm
concepts.statement: Heap's algorithm generates all n! permutations, each from the previous by a single swap, by a recursion that swaps a[k-1] with a[i] or a[0] according to the parity of k; recursive and iterative forms.
concepts.notes: E: pseudocode; the article continues with a proof and frequent mis-implementations.

concepts.name: Generating all subsets
concepts.statement: Decide for each element in turn whether it is in the subset (include, recurse, exclude, recurse); the 2^n leaves of this recursion are the subsets. Equivalently, the bits of each mask 0..2^n-1 select a subset (Solution 2).
concepts.notes: A/E: two models in one write-up (backtracking; binary enumeration). Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Subsets of a multiset
concepts.statement: Sort the input and, after excluding an element, skip its equal neighbours, so each distinct subset is generated once.
concepts.notes: A. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Subsets as bit strings
concepts.statement: Subsets of an n-element set correspond to functions from the set to {0, 1}, that is to n-bit strings, so counting from 0 to 2^n - 1 in binary enumerates every subset once.
concepts.notes: E (mathematical).

concepts.name: Power set: bitwise, backtracking and cascading
concepts.statement: Three ways to list the power set: read each number 0..2^n-1 as a bit mask, recurse with include/exclude decisions, or start from the empty set and add each element to every subset found so far.
concepts.notes: E: the README's Algorithms section only (MIT prose, ruling 12; the registry row says READMEs are not used, and the dossier clears this section as the author's own). Tests in __test__ are the registered use.

concepts.name: All subsets of a string
concepts.statement: Recurse from a start index, adding each remaining character with a positive count, recording the current result and backtracking, so each subset is produced once. O(2^n).
concepts.notes: A: the solution notebook's "## Algorithm" section (Apache-2.0 prose, ruling 12).

concepts.name: Generating k-combinations by backtracking
concepts.statement: Choose elements in increasing order: either decide pick or skip for each number, or loop the next pick from i to n; stop a branch when it can no longer reach k elements.
concepts.notes: A/E. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Combination sum with reuse
concepts.statement: Sort the candidates and recurse from index i, allowing the same candidate again; stop a branch as soon as a candidate exceeds the remaining target.
concepts.notes: A. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Enumerating k-combinations
concepts.statement: Track k index numbers starting from {1..k}; move to the next combination by incrementing the smallest index that can be incremented without colliding and resetting the smaller ones.
concepts.notes: E (short). Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Coin change: fewest coins by DP
concepts.statement: The fewest coins making value r is found by a table over coins and values: m[c][r] = min(m[c-1][r], 1 + m[c][r - coin_c]), with infinity where no change exists; the greedy method is optimal only for canonical coin systems.
concepts.notes: E: the DP, a Python implementation (CC BY-SA text), and the greedy method with when it fails (#Greedy method).

concepts.name: Change-making problem
concepts.statement: Greedy change works for canonical money systems; in general, try every coin P and solve the remaining amount X - P recursively, keeping the fewest coins, and memoise to avoid recomputing.
concepts.notes: E: OCaml code; carry the chapter's contributor credits.

concepts.name: Coin change as a complete knapsack
concepts.statement: f[i][j] is the fewest coins from the first i kinds making j: f[i][j] = min(f[i-1][j], f[i][j - x] + 1); Solution 2 rolls it into one array. O(mn).
concepts.notes: E/A: frames the problem as the complete knapsack (18.5). Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Minimum coins by memoised recursion
concepts.statement: For a total, try each coin not larger than it, recurse on the remainder, and keep the minimum plus one; memoise by total.
concepts.notes: A: the solution notebook's "## Algorithm" section (Apache-2.0 prose, ruling 12).

concepts.name: Coin change: counting the ways
concepts.statement: With dp[0] = 1, for each coin and each value i from the coin upward do dp[i] += dp[i - coin]; putting the coins in the outer loop counts each combination once regardless of order. O(N·S) time, O(N) space.
aliases: number of ways to make change
concepts.notes: E (MIT prose, ruling 12): with a worked table.

concepts.name: Ways to make change, one array
concepts.statement: arr[i] counts the ways to make i; for each coin and each index from coin to n, add arr[i - coin]; the notebook explains why adding a coin to the ways of making i - coin is correct.
concepts.notes: E: the solution notebook's "## Algorithm" section (Apache-2.0 prose, ruling 12).

concepts.name: Ways to make change, two-dimensional table
concepts.statement: T[i][j] = T[i-1][j] + T[i][j - coins[i]] counts the ways to make j with the first i coins; the answer is the bottom-right cell.
concepts.notes: A: the solution notebook's "## Algorithm" section (Apache-2.0 prose, ruling 12).

concepts.name: Coin change II as a complete knapsack count
concepts.statement: f[i][j] = f[i-1][j] + f[i][j - x] counts combinations; the loop order (coins outside) is what keeps permutations from being counted.
concepts.notes: E/A. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Counting grid paths
concepts.statement: The number of right/down paths to cell (i, j) is f[i][j] = f[i-1][j] + f[i][j-1] with f = 1 on the first row and column, so an m×n grid is counted in O(mn), and in O(n) memory with a rolling array; the count equals C(m+n-2, m-1).
concepts.notes: E/A: three DP solutions (plain, prefilled borders, rolling array). Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Unique paths: backtracking, DP and Pascal's triangle
concepts.statement: The decision tree of right/down moves gives an O(2^n) backtracking count; BOARD[i][j] = BOARD[i-1][j] + BOARD[i][j-1] gives O(mn); and the counts are entries of Pascal's triangle.
concepts.notes: E: the README's Algorithms section only (MIT prose, ruling 12); the opening problem statement and robot_maze.png are LeetCode's and link-only.

concepts.name: Counting lattice paths
concepts.statement: A north-east lattice path from (0, 0) to (n, k) is a sequence of n east and k north steps, so there are C(n+k, k) of them; the counts form Pascal's triangle.
concepts.notes: E (combinatorial); the figure File:Walking on Pascal's Triangle SVG.svg has an unchecked licence.

concepts.name: Lattice paths and binomial coefficients
concepts.statement: Paths on a grid moving only right and up correspond to bit strings with a fixed number of 1s, so a path to (m, n) is counted by C(m+n, n).
concepts.notes: E: lattice paths, bit strings and subsets as one count, with figures (part of the BY-SA text).

concepts.name: Counting grid paths around obstacles
concepts.statement: Set f[i][j] = 0 on obstacle cells and f[i][j] = f[i-1][j] + f[i][j-1] elsewhere; borders are filled until the first obstacle. O(mn).
concepts.notes: E/A: Solution 1 of the same write-up is memoised search. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: A robot's path around off-limits cells
concepts.statement: A cell is reachable if the cell to its left or the cell above is reachable and the cell is not off limits; memoised recursion from the target back to the start finds a path or reports none.
concepts.notes: A: the solution notebook's "## Algorithm" section (Apache-2.0 prose, ruling 12).

concepts.name: Minimum path sum in a grid
concepts.statement: f[i][j] = min(f[i-1][j], f[i][j-1]) + grid[i][j], with the first row and column as running sums; f[m-1][n-1] is the cheapest right/down path. O(mn).
concepts.notes: E/A. Solution write-up (CC BY-SA 4.0); the problem statement above it is LeetCode's and link-only, so the write-up is paired with an open exercise posing the same problem (ruling 15).

concepts.name: Family of Bachmann-Landau notations
concepts.statement: Big O, little o, Big Omega, little omega and Big Theta are defined side by side by limits and quantifiers: Theta(g) bounds f above and below, Omega(g) from below.
concepts.notes: E: comparison table. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Lower bounds and Theta notation
concepts.statement: Omega gives a lower bound on growth rate in the same way big-Oh gives an upper bound; when both bounds match, the cost is Theta of that function.
concepts.notes: E (MIT prose, ruling 12). Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Amortized analysis
concepts.statement: Amortized analysis bounds the cost of a sequence of operations rather than each one, so occasional expensive operations (dynamic array growth, two-stack queue transfers) are averaged over the cheap ones.
concepts.notes: E: the dynamic array and queue examples. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Amortized analysis
concepts.statement: The amortized cost of an operation is the total cost of a worst-case sequence divided by its length; potential and accounting arguments bound it.
concepts.notes: E (MIT prose, ruling 12). Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Aggregate, accounting and potential methods
concepts.statement: Three methods compute amortized cost: the aggregate method bounds the total of n operations; the accounting method charges cheap operations extra credit that pays for later expensive ones; the potential method uses a potential function of the state.
concepts.notes: E (short). Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Combinations and permutations
concepts.statement: Ordered selections of k from n number n!/(n-k)! and unordered ones C(n, k) = n!/(k!(n-k)!), told apart by whether order matters; worked with counting arguments.
concepts.notes: E (counting): listed in gap-patterns.md under generation as the counting background. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Permutation and combination numbers
concepts.statement: The number of arrangements of m of n distinct items is A(n, m) = n!/(n-m)!, and of selections C(n, m) = A(n, m)/m!.
concepts.notes: E. Chinese; usable in translation under docs/prompts/translate.md, AI-marked as a translation; SATA attribution thanks the OI Wiki authors (ruling 15). Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Array data structure
concepts.statement: An array stores elements of one size in contiguous memory so the address of element i is computed from the base address and i; multidimensional arrays map indices to one address by row-major or column-major order.
concepts.notes: E. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Arrays
concepts.statement: An array is a collection of elements reached in constant time by index; the chapter covers bounds, declaration, multidimensional arrays and growing arrays.
concepts.notes: E. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Linked list implementation
concepts.statement: A linked list is implemented from nodes holding an element and a next pointer, with head, tail and current pointers and a header node that removes special cases from insertion and removal.
concepts.notes: E (MIT prose, ruling 12): code with slideshows. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Queue on a linked list
concepts.statement: A queue implemented on a singly linked list enqueues at the tail and dequeues at the head, keeping a pointer to each end so both operations are O(1).
concepts.notes: E: the Queues section opens with the linked list implementation and its performance analysis. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Tail calls and tail recursion
concepts.statement: A call in tail position can reuse the caller's stack frame, so a tail-recursive function runs in constant stack space when the language eliminates tail calls; accumulators turn ordinary recursion into tail recursion.
concepts.notes: E. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Mathematical induction for correctness
concepts.statement: Prove a base case and that truth for n-1 implies truth for n; when the recursion shrinks the problem by more than one, assume the claim for all smaller values (strong induction).
concepts.notes: E: induction on a closed form and on a recursive algorithm, with strong induction. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Hash table
concepts.statement: A hash table maps keys to values through a hash function into an array of buckets, resolving collisions by chaining or open addressing; with a bounded load factor, operations take expected O(1) time.
concepts.notes: E. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Introduction to hashing
concepts.statement: Hashing finds a record by computing its slot from its key with a hash function into a table, rather than by comparisons; collisions must be resolved.
concepts.notes: E (MIT prose, ruling 12). Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Dynamic resizing of hash tables
concepts.statement: When the load factor passes a threshold the table is rebuilt at a larger size (typically doubled) and every entry rehashed; geometric growth keeps the amortized cost per insertion O(1).
concepts.notes: E. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Universal hashing
concepts.statement: A universal family of hash functions makes the probability that two distinct keys collide at most 1/m for a function drawn at random from it.
concepts.notes: E (short). Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Cuckoo hashing
concepts.statement: Cuckoo hashing keeps each key in one of two possible slots; an insertion that finds both full evicts an occupant to its alternative slot, giving worst-case constant lookups.
concepts.notes: E (short). Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Types and number representation
concepts.statement: IEEE 754 floating point splits a word into sign, exponent and significand, representing sign × significand × 2^exponent with a normalised significand, which limits precision.
concepts.notes: E: two's complement and floating point (CC BY-SA 3.0). Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Tree (abstract data type)
concepts.statement: A tree is a hierarchy of nodes with one root, each other node having exactly one parent; terminology (child, leaf, depth, height, subtree), operations and representations.
concepts.notes: E. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: General trees
concepts.statement: A general tree has a root and any number of subtrees per node; its ADT and traversals, with children kept by leftmost-child/right-sibling links.
concepts.notes: E (MIT prose, ruling 12). Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: BST successor and predecessor
concepts.statement: The successor of a node is the minimum of its right subtree if it has one; otherwise it is the lowest ancestor whose left subtree contains the node. Minimum and maximum follow left or right links to the end.
concepts.notes: E: pseudocode. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Self-balancing binary search tree
concepts.statement: A self-balancing BST restores small height (O(log n)) after insertions and deletions by local transformations such as rotations, so that operations stay logarithmic.
concepts.notes: E. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Balanced trees
concepts.statement: BST cost depends on depth; balance conditions (AVL, splay, 2-3) keep depth logarithmic without requiring perfect balance.
concepts.notes: E (MIT prose, ruling 12). Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Binary heap insert and extract
concepts.statement: Insertion appends at the bottom and sifts up (up-heap) while the parent is out of order; extraction moves the last element to the root and sifts down (down-heap), each O(log n).
concepts.notes: E. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Stability of sorting
concepts.statement: A stable sort keeps records with equal keys in their original relative order, which allows sorting by several keys in succession.
concepts.notes: E: playing-card example. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Selection sort
concepts.statement: Repeatedly select the smallest remaining element and swap it to the front: O(n^2) comparisons, at most n swaps, in place, not stable.
concepts.notes: E. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Selection sort
concepts.statement: The i-th pass selects the i-th smallest key and swaps it into position, so selection sort makes n-1 swaps and Theta(n^2) comparisons.
concepts.notes: E (MIT prose, ruling 12). Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Insertion sort
concepts.statement: Insert each element into its place in the sorted prefix by shifting larger elements right: O(n^2) worst case, O(n) on sorted input, stable and in place.
concepts.notes: E. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Insertion sort
concepts.statement: Each record is inserted into the sorted sublist before it by swapping it down; the cost is Theta(n^2) in the worst and average case and Theta(n) when the input is sorted.
concepts.notes: E (MIT prose, ruling 12). Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Bubble sort
concepts.statement: Repeatedly swap adjacent out-of-order elements, pass after pass, until no swap occurs: O(n^2), stable, with an early exit on sorted input.
concepts.notes: E. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Bubble sort
concepts.statement: Each pass bubbles the largest remaining key to its place by adjacent swaps; Theta(n^2) comparisons whatever the input.
concepts.notes: E (MIT prose, ruling 12). Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: AVL tree
concepts.statement: An AVL tree keeps the heights of every node's two subtrees within one, restoring the balance by single or double rotations after updates, so height is O(log n).
concepts.notes: E. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: AVL tree
concepts.statement: The AVL tree maintains the balance property by rotations after insertion and deletion; four rotation cases.
concepts.notes: E (MIT prose, ruling 12). Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: 2-3 tree
concepts.statement: A 2-3 tree is a search tree whose internal nodes have two children and one key or three children and two keys, with all leaves at one depth; insertion splits full nodes upward.
concepts.notes: E. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Splay tree
concepts.statement: A splay tree rotates each accessed node to the root by zig, zig-zig and zig-zag steps, giving O(log n) amortized cost per operation.
concepts.notes: E (MIT prose, ruling 12). Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: m-ary tree
concepts.statement: An m-ary tree is a rooted tree in which each node has at most m children; full, complete and perfect m-ary trees, their node counts and height bounds.
concepts.notes: E. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Trie operations
concepts.statement: Search, insertion and deletion in a trie follow one edge per key character, so they take time proportional to the key length, independent of the number of keys.
concepts.notes: E: pseudocode. Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Graph representations
concepts.statement: Adjacency lists, adjacency matrices and incidence matrices, with the time each takes for adding vertices and edges, removing them and testing adjacency.

concepts.name: Graph implementations

concepts.name: Bloom filter
concepts.statement: A Bloom filter sets k hashed bits per inserted element in an m-bit array; a query reports present if all k bits are set, giving no false negatives and a tunable false-positive rate.

concepts.name: Count-min sketch
concepts.statement: A count-min sketch keeps d rows of w counters with one hash function per row; each update increments one counter per row and a query returns the minimum, an overestimate bounded with high probability.

concepts.name: HyperLogLog
concepts.statement: HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct elements from the maximum number of leading zeros of hashed values in many registers, combined by a harmonic mean, using O(log log n) bits per register.

concepts.name: Locality-sensitive hashing
concepts.statement: Locality-sensitive hash families make similar items collide with higher probability than dissimilar ones, which turns approximate nearest-neighbour search into bucket lookups; random hyperplanes (simhash) and MinHash are examples.
concepts.notes: E (wp-sysdesign). Added to an existing concept; prerequisites are left to that concept's other rows.

concepts.name: Consistent hashing
concepts.statement: Mapping servers and keys onto a ring and assigning each key to the next server clockwise means adding or removing a server moves only about K/n keys; virtual nodes even out the load.

concepts.name: Distributed hash table
concepts.statement: A distributed hash table spreads key-value pairs across nodes with keyspace partitioning (often consistent hashing) and an overlay network that routes a lookup to the responsible node in few hops.

concepts.name: The Raft consensus algorithm (overview)
concepts.statement: Raft keeps a replicated log consistent by electing a leader that appends client commands and replicates them to a majority before committing; the page explains leader election and log replication.

concepts.name: Raft (algorithm)

concepts.name: Paxos
concepts.statement: Paxos lets a set of acceptors agree on one value despite failures: proposers run a prepare phase and an accept phase with ballot numbers, and a value chosen by a majority is never changed.

concepts.statement: Eight false assumptions newcomers make about distributed systems: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the network is secure, topology does not change, there is one administrator, transport cost is zero, the network is homogeneous.

concepts.statement: Redis is an in-memory key-value store with data structures (strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes), optional persistence and replication, used as a cache, message broker and database.

concepts.name: The NoSQL ecosystem
concepts.statement: NoSQL systems trade SQL's query model and transactions for data models (key-value, document, column-family, graph) and for partitioning and replication schemes such as consistent hashing and eventual consistency.
